posts.author: MarkCavin
posts.content_md:
Tonight I heated up my three day old batch of DCG, coated a bunch of microscope slides and made test shots then did a 4x5 quickie; I notice that most my DCGs come out with little green blotches so I have been trouble shooting. It sure feels nice not to worry about making expensive mistakes so I enjoy doing lots of test exposures without the stress of blowing a plate. I swear, every time I see a glass surface it has a Pavlovian effect.

Reprocessed Plate # 1 to see if I could go greener, it went redder. However, I did notice that under the laser it did replay fairly bright so I reason that I may not need to be as narrow and green as I thought to make single beam copies or even perhaps transmissions.

Looking forward to a photon rich weekend.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
> **MarkCavin:** Reprocessed Plate # 1 to see if I could go greener, it went redder.

Were your alcohol temperatures and concentrations the same as the first time? Did you dry it thouroughly after the last alcohol? 

I have never gotten a red shift on a reprocess, your going to have to share how you did that. 

Try this, but it may shift too blue. Reprocess again but after the last alcohol bath let the plate dry naturally leaned against a wall, no forced hot air.

That's the great thing about DCG. You can play for hours and reprocess quite a few time with the same plate.

Good luck on your next set of holograms.

posts.author: MarkCavin
posts.content_md:
John, I don’t know for sure what my temperatures are at this point. I only have one thermometer for my last bath; for the others I use the Mark 1 Mod 0 finger. It reports the baths to be right at about body temperature. The reprocessed plate only went slightly red, but in the past when I was working with Triple Takes plates I had several that where processed straight from the soak bath to hot 100 ISO and they came out a deep redish. 

Here is one of them.

![Image](http://home.wi.rr.com/cavin/owlDCG.jpg)

Of course I am still struggling with many tuning variables from beginning to finish. 

I don’t have running water in the Lab, Okay okay, it’s a garage, so I after fixer I rinse in a container of water then soak in another container of warm water for no more than 6 minutes; to complete my process I only use two or three baths, either 10/10-50/50-100/100 or 50/50-75/25-100/100 or 50/50-100/100. I notice that if my last bath is as hot as I can get it, I get the least number of green blotches on average.

The thing I get to witness is how everything changes everything. How I mix, how I coat, how I expose, how long I fix, how long I soak. I suspect that if a sparrow farted five miles south of Cape Horn; this would affect my final outcome. Its Awesome!!

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Mark, first I want to say I enjoy your humor. Lab mice, that was a good one.

Anyway your statement, "I suspect that if a sparrow farted five miles south of Cape Horn; this would affect my final outcome." is sooooo true.

It's not so bad, getting a set of proceedures down to replicate a type of DCG hologram. But go for a different effect and change one variable, and it seems 5 other variables need to be modified to make the one changed work. It is truely a medium for ones that like a challenge.

It IS awsome, and I love it.
